shows.title: Parataxis
shows.description:
Grace Weaver's seventh show with Galerie Max Hetzler brings together a new suite of paintings built around the small ceremonies of domestic life: figures and couples seated in chairs, gathered at tables, holding amphora-like vessels or raising a glass. Weaver flattens her interiors into bands of stripe and colour that read as panelling and doorways, so that the rooms feel less like real spaces than stages for repeated, ritualized gesture.

The title comes from the Greek for "placing side by side," and it describes both the compositional logic and the way bodies are handled here — legs merging into one in profile, heads reduced to near-perfect circles, torsos echoing the double-handled amphorae the figures carry. There's a debt to archaic and ancient sources (Mesopotamian seals, Mycenaean fresco blues, Trojan drinking vessels) filtered through a wet-into-wet painting technique that lets figure, ground and color arrive in a single pass rather than being built up in layers.

Alongside the large, left-to-right "scroll" paintings are a group of smaller, more economical works where a hand becomes a few decisive marks and a fingernail is a single fleck of paint — a useful contrast that shows how much Weaver can compress without losing the figure. The show runs concurrently with a presentation at Soy Capitán, and it's a good chance to see how a painter known for loose, expressive figuration has been tightening her forms toward something closer to hieroglyph or emblem.

shows.title: Kyiv Biennial: A Bird That Cannot Land
shows.description:
The Kyiv Biennial has never had a fixed home — since Russia's full-scale invasion forced it into exile, it has popped up in Warsaw, Antwerp, Dnipro, and Linz, among other cities — and this chapter turns KW's entire four-floor building over to its latest edition. More than 40 artists are packed into the show, ranging from internationally established names like Hito Steyerl, Mona Hatoum, and the late Geta Brătescu to younger Ukrainian, Central Asian, and Middle Eastern artists working in video, sound, sculpture, and performance.

The organizing idea is a loose geography the curators call "Middle-East-Europe," linking the post-Soviet East with Central and Southwest Asia and the Mediterranean — regions bound less by proximity than by shared histories of empire, displacement, and contested borders. Expect a lot of moving-image work and quietly devastating documentary material alongside more oblique, poetic pieces; the show leans hard into testimony and exile as subject matter without becoming a straightforward war-reportage exhibition.

Given Berlin's own large Ukrainian and Eastern European diaspora communities, staging this here rather than in a more neutral biennial city feels pointed, and KW has built out an unusually heavy parallel program of talks, screenings, and live performance alongside the galleries. It's a dense, demanding show — worth budgeting real time for — and one of the more substantial political-art statements in Berlin this year.

shows.title: Nachleben
shows.artist: Prinz Gholam, Hélène Delprat, Alma Feldhandler, Christa Joo Hyun D'Angelo, Jonas Weichsel, Rafael Domenech
shows.description:
Nachleben — Aby Warburg's term for the "afterlife" of an image or gesture that outlives its original occasion — gives this group show its working method rather than its subject. Each artist here acts as a kind of carrier through which an inherited picture, pose or grammar re-enters circulation altered. Prinz Gholam's four-handed drawings recall poses held in front of historical paintings years earlier, resurfacing from memory rather than reference; Hélène Delprat works by affinity across four decades of painting, film and installation, assembling a personal Mnemosyne Atlas of literature, radio and art history.

Alma Feldhandler's thinly layered paintings are fed by century-old diasporic and Victorian photographs without ever quoting them directly, while Christa Joo Hyun D'Angelo's neon text answers rather than repeats Audre Lorde's warning about silence. Jonas Weichsel pushes the inherited grammar of geometric abstraction until it yields sensations it was never built to produce, and Monilola Olayemi Ilupeju's work insists that some images survive not as homage but as evidence of injury.

It's a smart, tightly argued show for anyone interested in how historical images and gestures keep resurfacing in contemporary work without being merely appropriated or quoted — less a survey of influence than a demonstration of how form itself can carry memory forward.

shows.title: Parataxis
shows.description:
Grace Weaver's tall, sloping figures have become something of a signature — bodies compressed and elongated until they read almost as pictographs, engaged in the small ceremonies of domestic life: sitting, holding a vessel, gathering around a table. This show, jointly presented with Galerie Max Hetzler and opening during Berlin Art Week, brings together new paintings built on that vocabulary, with the ceremonial gravity of the scenes constantly undercut by a dry, formal humor — two legs merging into one in profile, a head reduced to a near-perfect circle.

The title, Parataxis, borrows a grammatical term for placing clauses side by side without subordinating connectors, and it describes Weaver's compositional method well: figures, furniture and architecture are compressed into a shallow pictorial field where everything sits in visual rhyme rather than illusionistic depth — a shoulder echoing the curve of a handle, a chair back mirroring a stiffened spine. Cobalt blues drawn from Mycenaean frescoes and the swelling profiles of Trojan drinking vessels give the domestic scenes an unexpected art-historical undertow, as if ordinary rituals were being restaged with the formal weight of antiquity.

Weaver, who is based between New York and Berlin, has built a substantial institutional profile in recent years, including solo shows at Kunstmuseum Magdeburg and Neues Museum Nürnberg and works entering the Städel Museum's collection — this show is a good measure of how her figuration has matured, trading loose gesture for a tighter, more architectonic sense of color and form.

shows.title: Der Titel kommt zuletzt (The Title Comes Last)
shows.description:
Kerim Seiler fills Sexauer's Weißensee space with three large works built around the idea of space as a stage rather than a container. On the floor, the sprawling installation "Tschutschu" seats more than a hundred people at once, turning the gallery into a literal meeting point; overhead, the neon piece "Spaceknot (News)" hangs like a line drawing suspended in the room; and across one wall, roughly a hundred framed ink drawings — the "Holotypes" — form a strict grid of Rorschach-like forms.

Seiler works out of a Situationist lineage, treating the exhibition itself as a site for drift and encounter rather than a fixed sequence of objects to view in order — his own line for it is "space is my canvas." The ink drawings carry a sly twist: he ran all 105 motifs through an AI program tasked with inventing a fictional viewer's interpretation of each one, then printed that invented reading on the back of the corresponding work, so visitors can compare their own projections against a machine's.

It's a show that resists being pinned to a single narrative by design — the title arrives only after the fact, per Seiler's own framing, because what happens in the space (who sits where, who meets whom) determines what the work turns out to mean. Worth the trip out past the Ring to see how a single artist can turn drawing, neon and furniture-scale sculpture into one continuous argument about attention and presence.

shows.title: in between Sommer 2026
shows.artist: Arnulf Rainer, Hans Uhlmann, Heimrad Prem, Horst Antes, Ida Kerkovius, Konrad Klapheck, Marwan, Michael Langer, Ursula (Schultze-Bluhm), Uwe Lausen, Werner Heldt
shows.description:
A late-summer group hang drawn from Galerie Michael Haas's deep stock in German post-war painting and sculpture, "in between Sommer 2026" is the kind of survey show that lets a gallery show its hand: figuration and gesture running from the 1940s through the 1970s. Horst Antes's blocky, totemic "Kopffigur," Werner Heldt's melancholic townscape, and a bronze by the sculptor Hans Uhlmann sit alongside Constructivist-adjacent abstraction from Ida Kerkovius and the raw, expressive brushwork of Uwe Lausen and Heimrad Prem, two artists associated with Munich's SPUR group.

Konrad Klapheck, known for his cool, machine-derived Pop paintings, contributes a more recent canvas ("The Ladies," 2012), giving the show a hinge between mid-century German modernism and its later inheritors. Arnulf Rainer's overpainted "Irma la Douce" and Ursula's fantastical, folkloric scene round out a compact but wide-ranging survey — less a thematic argument than a chance to see how differently German painters of the postwar decades handled the human figure and the urban and domestic worlds around them.

shows.title: Green Sanctuary (C.O.T.B)
shows.description:
Veit Laurent Kurz has built his practice around fiction and invented mythology, but this show — mounted alongside Haus am Waldsee's 80th-anniversary exhibition — turns him toward something closer to field research. C.O.T.B stands for "Circle of the Bee," an ongoing project that mixes ecological observation, historical digging and a speculative bee's-eye view of the world, and here it's trained on the institution's own garden: a landscape that reads as natural but is, like any English-style garden, a carefully composed cultural artifact.

Seven research posters function as a kind of pseudo-scientific dossier alongside the sculptural and image-based works, which include a series of ceramic "Bee Fountains" that fuse hive and watering trough into hybrid forms recalling coral or mold spores. The effect is a deliberate destabilization of scale and viewpoint — you're invited to imagine the garden as an insect would experience it, which turns a familiar sculpture park into something stranger and more provisional.

It's a smart pairing with the "Wo ich wohne" show next door: where that exhibition excavates the house's human history, Kurz digs into the ecological and ideological history of its grounds.

shows.title: Wo ich wohne
shows.description:
Haus am Waldsee turns 80 this year, and rather than mount a straightforward retrospective of past exhibitions, it has built a show out of the building itself. Constructed in 1922 as a private villa and repurposed as an exhibition space since 1946, the house becomes both subject and site: works by Nigin Beck, Rhea Dillon, Robert Haas, Hannah Höch, Patrick Jolly & Reynold Reynolds, Alexandre Khondji, Atiéna R. Kilfa, Henry Koerner, Yoora Park, Oskar Schlemmer, Renée Sintenis, Ian Waelder and Frau von Zinowiew are threaded through the rooms alongside a large new architectural intervention by Richard Venlet.

Some of the pieces on view were actually shown here in the institution's early years and are returning after decades away, while newer commissions respond directly to the traces of domestic life still legible in the building — door frames, sightlines, the ghost of furniture arrangements. It's as much an exercise in institutional self-examination as an art exhibition, using the vocabulary of habitation (who lived here, who exhibited here, what remains) to think through what a Kunsthalle actually is once you strip away the white cube fiction.

Curated by director Anna Gritz with Pia-Marie Remmers, the show anchors a season of anniversary programming, including performances and curator-led tours scheduled through late September.

shows.title: Fischmond am Waldsee
shows.description:
A quiet, long-durational counterpart to the anniversary exhibitions inside, "Fischmond am Waldsee" is a sound walk by violinist and sound artist Ayumi Paul threaded through the institution's sculpture garden. Nine stones, each engraved with a fish-in-a-moon symbol, mark a path that visitors follow while listening to a composition built from the garden's own pre-dawn birdsong.

Paul's work draws on oral history and personal memory as much as field recording — the piece is framed as an evocation of the friendships that have shaped this landscape over time, tying it to migratory routes of plants and animals as well as human visitors. Media players are available at the front desk for anyone without a personal device, and the piece rewards a slow, unhurried circuit of the garden rather than a quick pass-through.

It's a low-key but well-judged complement to the more object-heavy shows on view this season, using the Waldsee's own grounds — lake, trees, sculpture park — as the actual exhibition space.

shows.title: Hanglage
shows.description:
Hanglage is Eric Keller's fifth solo show at Galerie Poll, and it continues a project he's been quietly building for years: painting the abandoned Kulturhäuser of the former GDR. These are the empty ballrooms and function halls once built for collective leisure — faded stage curtains, dusty stage sets, forgotten paper garlands, orphaned chairs — places that now read as both eerie and strangely tender, haunted by a vanished form of collective sociability. Keller renders them in thin, layered oil glazes, building up washed-out or clouded, almost dissolving abstractions where it's never quite clear whether you're looking at a wall or a picture within the picture.

Alongside the interiors, the show brings in unglamorous urban spaces — towpaths, sports grounds, parking lots, railway crossings — and a smaller group of figure paintings based on drawn portrait studies of friends. Since 2023 Keller's horizons have widened beyond his native Saxony to include impressions from trips to South Korea and the Canary Islands, and two large-format canvases in the show, set near Gunsan and Teguise, extend the palimpsest-like method to new geographies while keeping the same muted grays, blues, violets and ochres.

Keller, born in Grimma in 1985, trained in Nuremberg, Dresden and Leipzig, finishing as a Meisterschüler under Annette Schröter at Leipzig's Hochschule für Grafik und Buchkunst. A 2025 Kunstfonds stipend allowed him to keep developing the Kulturhäuser series, which will get its first institutional outing at the Städtische Galerie Dresden's project space in early 2027 — making this Berlin show a useful preview of where the work is headed.

shows.title: After Memory. Echoes in the Future Perfect Tense
shows.description:
This international group show treats memory itself as a battleground. Curated by Lisa Deml, Nathalia Lavigne and Víctor Fancelli Capdevila, it brings together fourteen artists — Noor Abuarafeh, Heba Y. Amin, Maria Thereza Alves, Aram Bartholl, Taysir Batniji, Giselle Beiguelman, Zach Blas, Karolina Grzywnowicz, Ana Hupe, Eduardo Kac, Aline Motta, Rabih Mroué, the duo Vanessa Amoah Opoku & Joy Weinberger, and Federico Protto — who each approach remembering and forgetting as political acts rather than neutral cognitive functions.

The premise is pointed: in an era when data extraction, algorithmic curation and disinformation campaigns actively reshape what gets remembered and by whom, artists working across video, installation, photography and archival material have unusual leverage to counter-narrate. The show doesn't treat digital technology only as a threat to memory, either — several works explore how the same networked tools that enable surveillance and erasure can also be repurposed for resistant, collective forms of remembrance.

Given the range of geographies and histories represented — from Palestine to Brazil to Poland — the exhibition works less as a single argument than as a chorus of case studies in how memory gets contested, weaponized and reclaimed. It's a substantial, research-driven show typical of Kunstraum Kreuzberg/Bethanien's ongoing focus on socially engaged, internationally minded group projects.

shows.title: 매난국죽 Mae Nan Guk Juk: Diasporic Memories Formed in Clay
shows.description:
Frank Jimin Hopp's exhibition takes up a piece of migration history that rarely gets told: the South Koreans recruited to West Germany as miners and nurses in the 1960s and '70s under bilateral labor agreements, whose contribution to the country's postwar economy has been largely written out of the mainstream memory of migration to Germany. Working with members of that first generation, Hopp conducted interviews reconstructing memories of migration, care work, loss, friendship and new beginnings, then developed a parallel body of ceramic objects alongside them — the slow, hands-on process of shaping clay becoming a way of drawing out and holding these life stories.

The result is a show built from two intertwined bodies of work: video pieces carrying the interviews themselves, and a wide array of ceramic objects that emerged from the collaborative making sessions. The title refers to the "four noble plants" of East Asian painting tradition — plum blossom, orchid, chrysanthemum and bamboo — symbols of resilience, dignity and steadfastness that Hopp repurposes here as emblems of diasporic memory and survival.

Hopp, born in Berlin in 1994 to a Korean-German family, studied under Leiko Ikemura and is currently in Valérie Favre's class at the UdK Berlin, with additional study at the Universidad Complutense de Madrid and University of the Arts London. His work has been shown at Haus am Kleistpark, Gropius Bau, Künstlerhaus Bethanien and the Saatchi Gallery, and he won the Haus am Kleistpark's 2019 art prize. Curated by Eylem Sengezer, the show treats the ceramic works as a living archive — one that keeps expanding through encounter and retelling rather than sitting fixed as a historical record.

shows.title: Materie unter Materie (Matter Beneath Matter)
shows.description:
Malwine Stauss's second solo show at Jarmuschek + Partner gathers new watercolors and glazed ceramics populated by a private bestiary of angels, humans, snails, shells and invented creatures, all seemingly adrift in the same watery, sand-strewn world. Figures wrestle, sink into dunes, or dissolve into the sea — the paintings read like fragments of a longer, half-legible story rather than isolated scenes.

Stauss, who trained in illustration in Leipzig and has published several artist's books, works in a fragile, watercolor-based idiom that owes something to the ecological and post-humanist thinking of writers like Ursula K. Le Guin and Robin Wall Kimmerer: the title translates roughly as "matter beneath matter," and the show is essentially an argument for seeing the self as one small, permeable part of a larger continuum of materials and beings, rather than as anything separate from them.

It's a gentle, intimate show, best suited to close looking — the appeal is in the tenderness of the watercolor surfaces and the way Stauss gives equal weight to a jellyfish, a hand, and a fold of fabric.

shows.title: Counterplay
shows.description:
Alicja Rogalska's Counterplay grows out of her multi-year engagement with Berlin's bike courier workforce, extending a line of research that began with the two-channel video Terms and Conditions at n.b.k. in 2024. Rather than simply document the precarity of platform-based gig work, Rogalska turns her collaborators into co-authors of speculative fictions: couriers appear here not just as subjects of exploitation but as agents imagining alternative economic systems, using games and role-play as tools of collective world-building.

The exhibition unfolds across video, installation and game-like objects, including material from a cooperative board-game-development workshop the artist has run with participants. It sits alongside a dense public programme — artist and curator walkthroughs, a panel on economic science fiction, and a session on platform capitalism featuring labor organizers and researchers — that treats the gallery as a working space for building the "counterplay" of the title rather than a passive viewing room.

Rogalska, a Polish-British artist based between Berlin and London, has a research-driven practice that stages situations and performances in collaboration with communities whose labor or history she is examining; her work has appeared at the Zachęta National Gallery, the Jogja Biennale and Urbane Künste Ruhr. Curated by Jorgina Stamogianni, the show is a good example of Galerie Nord's ongoing interest in socially engaged, dialogic art practice.

shows.title: Genius Loci XIII
shows.description:
Now in its thirteenth edition, Genius Loci is SETAREH's long-running curatorial platform for artists working close to a given place, and this installment — the first ever staged in Berlin rather than Düsseldorf — turns that lens on the city itself. Curated by Berlin-based artist Allistair Walter in his first outing as a curator, the show brings together thirteen painters, sculptors and ceramicists who are all active in the city's current scene: Vasil Berela, Johannes Bosisio, Jascha Froh, Lisa Götze, Lara Koch, Merlin Luczynski, Anja Rausch, Richard Roberts, Alec Ross, Alex See, Julian Simon, Jill Winnie and Marco Żebrowski.

Rather than imposing a single theme, Walter has grouped artists who share a sensibility for suspension and ambiguity — works caught between finished and unfinished, presence and absence. That plays out across very different materials: Vasil Berela's oil paintings and unsettling silicone-and-textile figures sit alongside Anja Rausch's blunt, fleshy canvases, Merlin Luczynski's glazed and oxide-inked clay vessels, Lara Koch's water-and-brass sculpture, and Alec Ross's carved wood pieces embedded with pine resin and coal.

Painting dominates numerically — Johannes Bosisio's masked self-portraits, Julian Simon's diptych panels, Richard Roberts's acrylic-and-oil landscapes, Jill Winnie's bead- and sequin-flecked canvases — but the show reads less as a painting survey than as a snapshot of a generation working through instability as a working condition rather than a crisis, a framing that feels pointed given the funding cuts and closures that have unsettled Berlin's gallery scene over the past year.

It's a useful show for anyone trying to get a read on younger Berlin-based artists who haven't yet settled into a single gallery's roster — thirteen distinct practices, loosely but deliberately arranged, in a space built for exactly this kind of survey.

shows.title: In Between
shows.description:
Jonathan Binet's first Berlin solo show gathers a tight body of recent paintings built from a working method that treats accident as material. Rather than starting from a fixed image, Binet lets studio incidents — stray marks, drips, scrapes, and the residue of earlier canvases — steer where a picture lands, so each untitled panel reads as a record of decisions made and un-made in real time.

Color plays an unusually active role here compared to Binet's earlier, more monochrome-leaning work: flat grounds get interrupted by sudden hot patches or thin washes that behave less like composition than like disruption. One piece in the show pushes the premise furthest — a fragment cut directly from the studio wall, its buildup of years of overspray and splatter presented as a finished painting in its own right, blurring the line between by-product and artwork.

Binet trained in Paris and Saint-Étienne and has shown at Palais de Tokyo, Bonner Kunstverein, and Balice Hertling, among others; this exhibition extends a practice that treats painting as an open-ended inquiry rather than an illustration of a predetermined idea. It rewards close, slow looking — the kind of attention the paintings themselves seem to have required to make.

shows.title: How Can Language Be Found in the Body?
shows.description:
This two-person exhibition pairs a Mexican sculptor with a Berlin performance artist around a shared question: what physically happens to a body as it absorbs a new language. Francisco Diego contributes deformed, body-adjacent bronze sculptures — objects that look stressed or bent as if they'd been worn — while Stella Geppert brings her long-running interest in embodied, non-verbal communication, staged here through sculptural props and performative encounters rather than text or speech.

The two artists work from opposite ends of the same problem. Diego's practice leans on technical sculptural and graphic craft rooted in figurative traditions, translating conceptual ideas about memory and translation into solid, weighted forms. Geppert works live and provisionally, using body-worn constructions to enact specific physical states in front of an audience; her past projects have moved through venues from Copenhagen's Dansehallerne to the Liu Haisu Art Museum in Shanghai. Together at rosalux, their collaboration folds in a digital-fabrication twist — sculptures and molds are scanned, exchanged as files between the two artists' distant studios, and rematerialized, leaving printer-layer traces as visible evidence of that back-and-forth translation.

The show runs through Berlin Art Week, with an extra public opening on September 6 timed to that citywide event, plus tours, an artist talk, and a finissage — reflecting rosalux's project-space format of dense, short-run public programming around a single presentation rather than a long static hang.

shows.title: DIALOGUE – Collection Presentation
shows.artist: Leiko Ikemura, Lee Ufan, Lee Bae, Leena Luostarinen
shows.description:
This is the inaugural exhibition in the Miettinen Collection's newly renovated fourth-floor space, built around a long-running affinity in the collection between Finnish art and East Asian art — a kinship the wall text frames not as a curatorial theme but as something closer to an instinct, traced back to the shared reticence and material sensitivity of Nordic and Japanese modernism.

Four artists carry the show. Leiko Ikemura, who grew up between Japan, Spain, Switzerland and Germany, contributes paintings, sculpture and drawing built around shifting, unstable figures that read more as states of being than portraits. Lee Ufan, co-founder of the Mono-ha movement, is represented with the spare, gestural vocabulary — a single brushstroke, a single stone — that made him one of postwar Asian art's most influential figures, while his younger countryman Lee Bae extends that lineage through charcoal-based works whose dense blacks carry an unexpected sense of fullness and material memory. The late Finnish painter Leena Luostarinen (1949–2013) rounds out the group with her vividly colored, symbol-laden canvases of big cats, sphinxes and lotus flowers, drawn from a lifetime of travel and cross-cultural looking.

Rather than a comprehensive survey marking the reopening, the collection chose to show the artists closest to its own identity — a quieter, more personal way of inaugurating the new rooms. It's worth seeing both for the individual strength of the works (particularly the Ikemura and Lee Ufan pieces) and as a window into how a private collection's taste gets built over decades.

shows.title: Nach Bild (Under Stimulation)
shows.description:
Vinzenz Aubry's first solo exhibition turns the gallery into a set of participatory rigs rather than a wall hang of finished pictures. Infrasound generators, afterimage-inducing light, and a patch of astroturf turn visitors into the actual subject matter: you have to lie down, stand still, or let your retina be worked on before anything like an "image" resolves. The show's premise is blunt — that a culture saturated in images has lost any stable relationship to the visible, and that the way back is through the body rather than through more pictures.

The installations on view include a sunken screen showing NASA solar footage, blue geometric walk-through structures, and a green-carpeted lounging area where the exhibition itself becomes a place to linger rather than pass through. It's less a display of objects than a set of thresholds — Aubry keeps referring to "open works" that only complete themselves once someone steps into them.

It's a strong choice for anyone tired of didactic photography or video art: this is sensory and a little disorienting by design, closer to a low-fi immersive environment than a conventional gallery show, and it rewards showing up in person rather than looking at documentation.

shows.title: Die kochenden Affen (The Cooking Apes)
shows.description:
Tine Steen's exhibition translates her nonfiction comic Die kochenden Affen — a 300-page graphic history of cooking as an engine of human evolution — into a room full of slightly larger-than-life cardboard characters. Homo erectus, bonobos, an Australopithecus, chimpanzees and a handful of researchers all appear as hand-built figures whose limbs pivot on simple lever mechanisms, so that a visitor can set them chewing, cooking, showing off or begging. Seen from the front they reproduce the comic's flat, colorful drawing style; walk around them and the illusion breaks, exposing raw cardboard structure and the hardware that animates them — some of it literally cut from supermarket food packaging, which keeps the deep-time subject tethered to the everyday act of grocery shopping.

Steen, a Berlin-based painter and comic author who trained under Per Kirkeby at the Städelschule, spent years working across painting, textiles and installation before turning to comics around 2020; this is the exhibition extension of her first graphic book, published by avant-verlag in 2025 and a finalist for the Berthold Leibinger comic prize. The show is a brief coda to a public reading and artist talk held the night before — it runs for just two afternoons, so this is very much a catch-it-now proposition rather than something to pencil in for later in the month.

shows.title: What Still Holds
shows.description:
Shilpa Gupta has built a three-decade career out of making the intangible — censorship, borders, surveillance, the fragility of memory — physically felt, and this survey-scale presentation inside the Kleihues Halle is her biggest German museum outing yet. The anchor is TRUTH, a room-filling sculpture of oversized freestanding letters that visitors have to walk between and around, turning an abstract word into an obstacle course. It's a blunt, almost comic gesture that becomes unsettling the longer you sit with it: what does it mean to physically navigate the idea of truth in a building that has itself served, at different points in history, very different political purposes?

Around that centerpiece, the show gathers pieces spanning Gupta's career-long interest in language as a site of control and resistance — hand-drawn maps redrawn from memory, a library of books published anonymously or under pseudonyms, sound and text works that toy with what can and can't be said aloud. Mumbai-born and based, Gupta has shown at the Barbican, MAXXI, and Centro Botín, and won the 2025 Possehl Prize for International Art; this is the kind of mid-career museum show that clarifies why she keeps getting invited back.

What makes the presentation especially sharp is its staging: it runs in deliberate dialogue with Hamburger Bahnhof's permanent Joseph Beuys collection display next door, the fourth time the museum has paired a woman artist against that canonical room. Beuys treated language and social sculpture as inseparable; Gupta, working from a very different political vantage point, asks similar questions about who gets to speak and be believed. Seeing the two shows back to back, as the museum clearly intends, is the most interesting way to spend an afternoon at Hamburger Bahnhof's 30th-anniversary program this year.

shows.title: Repose
shows.description:
David Claerbout has spent three decades pulling video and photography apart at the seams of time, and this second solo show with Esther Schipper gathers four recent works that push that project to extremes of duration. The centerpiece, The Woodcarver and the Forest (2025), pairs a twenty-hour looped video installation with black-and-white photographic prints of a lone, bearded lumberjack set against a forest he treats as an inexhaustible resource — a quietly damning image of the fantasy of "returning to nature" in a culture that mediates every experience of the wild. Eagle Eye (2026), a silent single-channel video running seven and a half hours, and Backwards Growing Tree (2023), a video projection looped over five years, extend the same interest in near-imperceptible change: images that look still until you notice, much later, that something has moved.

Birdcage (2023), a shorter looped video just under an hour and a half, and a group of new ink, pastel and gouache works on paper round out the exhibition, giving a more intimate, hand-made counterpoint to the glacial video pieces. Claerbout, born in 1969 in Kortrijk and trained originally as a painter, has always worked in the gap between photography's frozen instant and film's flow of time; here that gap becomes the whole subject, with drawings that function almost like storyboards or afterimages of the moving works nearby.

The show's title, Repose, is a fitting frame: nothing here moves quickly, and the works reward exactly the kind of patient, unhurried looking that repose implies. It's a good entry point for anyone curious why Claerbout is treated as one of the more rigorous voices working at the border of video art and cinema — his pieces are less about spectacle than about recalibrating how long you're willing to watch something that barely changes.

Esther Schipper's Potsdamer Strasse space reopens for the new season with this show alongside a concurrent presentation of Tuan Andrew Nguyen's sculpture, making early September a strong moment to catch both emerging and established positions on the gallery's roster.

shows.title: Never Forget: September 11, 2001
shows.description:
Timed to the 25th anniversary of the attacks, this group exhibition gathers more than forty photographs tracing how photojournalists and art photographers alike responded to September 11, 2001. Thomas Hoepker's widely reproduced (and long debated) view of young New Yorkers on the Williamsburg waterfront with smoke rising behind them anchors the show, alongside Magnum-archive material, Pete Souza's images of the Pentagon in the attack's immediate aftermath, and Elliott Erwitt's earlier, more elegiac view of the World Trade Center towers standing over the city.

Rather than a straightforward documentary chronicle, the show is built around the idea that the World Trade Center itself has been a recurring subject across decades of photographic history — so alongside images made in the attack's direct aftermath, curators have folded in pictures made years before 2001 that frame the towers as skyline icons, giving the exhibition an unusual double perspective on a moment that redefined how the city, and the buildings themselves, would be remembered.

For a commercial gallery best known for celebrity portraiture and fashion photography, this is a more sober undertaking, treating photojournalism's role in constructing collective memory as seriously as it treats the aesthetics of a single iconic frame.

shows.title: Ausstellung realisiert durch seine Tochter Anna Tripamer
shows.description:
This is the fourth exhibition of the late Austrian artist Walter Pichler (1936–2012) at Contemporary Fine Arts, and the first to be conceived and installed by his daughter Anna Tripamer, who oversaw the artist's estate and was a close witness to his working process. Pichler made his name in the 1960s with the "Prototypes" — futuristic body-and-space works built from then-radical synthetic materials like PVC, acrylic and aluminum — before withdrawing from the international art world in the early 1970s to a farmstead in rural Burgenland, on the border with Slovenia and Hungary.

There he shifted entirely to organic materials — wood, brick, clay, glass, lead — and spent the following decades producing sculptures, drawings and models with an obsessive, almost devotional slowness, often building simple houses on his property expressly to shelter individual sculptures. He treated architecture and sculpture as inseparable, and refused for most of his life to sell or exhibit work that had already found a "home" in one of these structures.

This presentation offers a concentrated look at that singular, self-contained universe — drawings, models and sculptural objects that show an artist whose radical rejection of the gallery-and-museum system only deepened the intensity of the work itself. Given Pichler's own resistance to exhibiting, and the rarity of seeing his work outside Austria, this is a notable opportunity to encounter it in Berlin.

shows.title: de sensu
shows.description:
"de sensu" — Latin for "through the senses" — is Leiko Ikemura's second solo show at the gallery's Berlin space, bringing together new paintings and glazed ceramic and terracotta figures built around the idea of perception as something felt through the whole body, not just seen. Three green-toned figures, titled "Green Baby," "Green Mom" and "Dear Spirit," anchor the installation, staged against green walls and accents of yellow and dark blue light meant to evoke the threshold between day and night.

Ikemura, who has lived and worked in Berlin since the 1980s and taught painting at the city's University of the Arts for over two decades, works in a register that moves between childlike vulnerability and mythic strangeness — hybrid, often female figures that merge human and animal traits, most famously her recurring rabbit-eared "Usagi," first created in response to the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Her new sculpture "Milk Lady" continues this interest in bodies as vessels of care and transformation, absorbing and releasing energy in a cycle without clear beginning or end.

Trained in Osaka and Seville before settling in Europe, Ikemura draws on Japanese ink painting traditions, European Surrealism and postwar abstraction in equal measure, and her hybrid creatures have made her one of the more distinctive figurative artists working in Germany today — recognition that culminated last year in Japan naming her a "Person of Cultural Merit."

shows.title: Love is the work
shows.description:
Rachel Seidu's first show at Between Bridges brings her documentary-rooted photographic practice to the foundation's Kreuzberg space. Working out of Nigeria, Seidu has built a body of work around queer intimacy, faith, and community life that resists the sensationalism often applied to LGBTQIA+ subjects in West Africa, instead favoring tenderness, dignity and everyday gesture.

The title, "Love is the work," reads as both a statement of method and of politics: Seidu treats the act of photographing her subjects as an extension of care and solidarity rather than observation from a distance. Images such as her "Sacraments of Recognition" series place her sitters in quiet, almost devotional compositions, borrowing the visual language of portraiture and ritual to assert a plain claim to visibility and belonging.

Shown in a foundation established by Wolfgang Tillmans around humanism, solidarity and LGBTQIA+ rights, the exhibition extends Between Bridges' pattern of platforming younger photographers whose work sits at the intersection of activism and image-making. It's a compact but pointed show worth catching during Berlin Art Week.

shows.title: Horizontal Fold
shows.description:
Andreas Eriksson's paintings and prints have long circled a single, stubborn subject: the forest and fields around his home in Medelplana, Sweden, reduced and refracted until the landscape becomes almost abstract. Horizontal Fold gathers new work built from that same source material — folded, layered, and flattened views of the land that read alternately as topography, weather, or pure pattern. The show's screenprints and paintings share a horizontal pull, as if the land itself were being pressed flat and stacked like sediment.

Installation views from the gallery's two rooms show large panel works alongside a big-scale veranda-facing installation, suggesting a show built as much around architecture and light as around individual pictures. Eriksson has exhibited widely across Scandinavia and Germany, and his work sits comfortably between the traditions of Nordic landscape painting and a more contemporary interest in surface, repetition, and printmaking process.

Notably, the exhibition is staged in tandem with a parallel show at neugerriemschneider, where Eriksson is paired with the Korean painter Kim Chong Hak — a rare instance of two Berlin galleries mounting complementary halves of a single artist's moment, timed to Berlin Art Week. Seeing both makes for a fuller picture of an artist who keeps finding new ways to say the same quiet thing about a particular patch of land.

shows.title: Sediments
shows.description:
Berlin-based painter Clemens Krauss has built his reputation on thickly worked, impasto canvases exploring the tension between the individual body and the collective, and with "Sediments" he turns that same heavy, geological application of oil paint toward a new subject: buildings, surfaces and everyday objects rather than the human figure. The shift reframes his signature technique — layer built on layer of paint, worked and reworked until the surface reads almost like relief sculpture — as a literal analogue for the way architecture and material accumulate history over time.

Krauss treats the city itself as a kind of sedimentary record, with stone, concrete, clay and water each carrying their own material memory, compressed and re-exposed the way his paint layers reveal earlier colors breaking through later ones. He connects this way of thinking explicitly to psychoanalysis, drawing on Freud's idea that the ego originates in bodily sensation, and reading the buried strata of a painted surface as analogous to the buried strata of a repressed or half-remembered past.

The result is a body of work that sits between abstraction and observed urban reality — thick, tactile paintings that reward close viewing for the way light catches their built-up ridges and valleys, while still resolving, at a distance, into recognizable fragments of architecture and object.

shows.title: Fire Sermon
shows.description:
Fire Sermon is Vietnamese-American artist Tuan Andrew Nguyen's first solo exhibition with Esther Schipper, bringing five new sculptures from his ongoing series of mobiles into the gallery's Berlin space. Nguyen is best known for cinematic work that braids oral history, colonial memory, and material culture across Vietnam and its diaspora, and these hanging sculptures extend that same interest in storytelling into three dimensions — objects built to turn slowly in the air, catching light and shifting relationships between their parts as they move.

Trained at UC Irvine and a co-founder of the Ho Chi Minh City collective The Propeller Group, Nguyen has built a practice around community-based research and the long afterlives of conflict, migration, and material history. His sculptural work has always run parallel to his films rather than illustrating them, and this show is a chance to see that strand on its own terms, freed from narrative voiceover.

Opening during Berlin Art Week alongside David Claerbout's Repose in the gallery's other rooms, Fire Sermon marks a first collaboration between Nguyen and the gallery worth catching for anyone who has followed his video work and wants to see how the same ideas translate into hanging, physical form.

shows.title: Follow the White Rabbit
shows.artist: Heike Buchfelder, MK Kaehne, Gisbert Pöppler, K.R.H. Sonderborg, Walter Stöhrer
shows.description:
Follow the White Rabbit stakes out the territory between art and design, pairing gestural postwar abstraction with contemporary collectible furniture. On one side are paintings and works on paper by K.R.H. Sonderborg and Walter Stöhrer, two figures associated with European Informel and gestural abstraction, their marks reading like frozen movement. On the other are Gisbert Pöppler's sculptural dining tables, consoles, and cast-aluminium furniture, along with Heike Buchfelder's folded glass and light objects and MK Kaehne's deadpan sculptural "products" — a wood-and-chrome pissoir chief among them.

The premise, spelled out in the gallery's own text, is that a table's polished surface can reflect and complete a nearby drawing, so that furniture and painting start to trade roles: the functional object becomes contemplative, and the wall work becomes almost usable. It's a curatorial idea that traces back to Meret Oppenheim's fur-lined teacup and runs forward through Duchamp and Warhol's blurring of art and product design.

The result is a show that rewards slow looking across mediums — drawings, ceramics, glass, cast metal, dyed cashmere — rather than one built around a single artist's development. It opens during Berlin Art Week with an artist-led walkthrough the following weekend.

shows.title: Collection Nothelfer: Selection of Works from the 1960s to the Present
shows.description:
Running alongside the gallery's main Berlin Art Week exhibition, this cabinet presentation is a walk through Galerie Georg Nothelfer's own holdings, spanning roughly sixty years of the program. Postwar gestural abstraction — Fred Thieler, Gerhard Hoehme, Walter Stöhrer, K.R.H. Sonderborg — sits alongside prints by Robert Motherwell, Richard Serra, and Christo & Jeanne-Claude, and more recent work by artists like Elmira Iravanizad, Mahdad Alizadeh, and Britta Lumer.

It's less a themed exhibition than a condensed house history, tracing a line from the gestural and scriptural painting the gallery has long championed through to ceramics, watercolor, and works on paper by a younger generation now on its roster. For visitors during Berlin Art Week, it functions as a useful primer on what this Charlottenburg-adjacent gallery has stood for since its founding, with enough variety in medium and period to reward a slow look around the cabinet room.

shows.title: Si quelque chose noir
shows.description:
This is the first exhibition in Germany devoted to Alix Cléo Roubaud (1952–1983), a Canadian-born photographer and writer who died at 31 having produced a small, fiercely uncompromising body of work almost entirely in a bathroom darkroom in her Paris apartment. Trained in philosophy under readings of Wittgenstein before turning to the camera, she treated photography less as documentation than as a way of testing the medium's own limits — building up high-key prints through multiple exposures, extensive dodging and burning, and what she called a "pencil of light," occasionally adding hand-tinting or colored pencil. She destroyed her negatives as she went, believing a negative should only be kept as long as it held living memory of the intended image — which means every surviving print is a unique object, not a reproducible edition.

The show, curated by Hélène Giannecchini, centers on Roubaud's major sequence "Si quelque chose noir" ("If Something Black"), the work in which her strange, self-erasing practice reached its fullest expression — an extended meditation on mortality and the fragility of the image made all the more charged by the fact that she died before the series found wide recognition (it was shown at Rencontres d'Arles only months after her death). The pictures are moody, high-contrast, often abstracted almost past the point of legibility, closer in spirit to the automatic writing of her Surrealist forebears than to conventional documentary photography.

Given how rarely Roubaud's prints circulate — her negatives don't exist to make new ones — this show is a genuine rarity, and a chance to encounter a photographer whose reputation has grown steadily since a wave of renewed institutional interest in France over the past decade.

shows.title: Second Echo
shows.description:
Second Echo pulls together roughly thirty years of Andy Hope 1930's work, threading paintings and objects from different decades around a shared set of obsessions: Suprematist geometry, science-fiction iconography, and a private mythology built from spaceships, black ovals, and gravitational fields. A large matte-black oval — described by the artist as a sequel to his 1997 Roswell Saucers — anchors the final room, while new 2026 paintings in the Second Echo and Untitled Sequences series apply spray technique and thick, built-up surfaces that nod as much to 1960s minimalist painting as to cosmic imagery.

Hope, who has shown internationally including at the 57th Venice Biennale, has always worked in a register that mixes high art references with pulp and comic-book sensibility — devils, dinosaurs, superheroes, and spacecraft recur across his output. Here that vocabulary gets a historical survey treatment, with black-sail motifs that trace back to his very first show at this gallery in 2001.

That anniversary is the real occasion for the exhibition: Second Echo marks both Hope's ninth solo show with Guido W. Baudach and the gallery's own 25th year, making this as much a milestone exhibition as a new body of work.

shows.title: Μέτοικε
shows.description:
Wu Tsang's new show at Isabella Bortolozzi takes its title from a Greek word for a resident foreigner, a metic — someone who lives in a place without full citizenship, caught between belonging and exclusion. That in-between status has been a throughline in Tsang's work for over a decade, from her documentary and fiction hybrids on trans and immigrant communities to her large-scale performance collaborations with boychild as Moved by the Motion.

Since her breakthrough film Wildness and her 2016 Berlin Biennale presentation at KW, Tsang has moved fluidly between museum-scale installation (Of Whales at the Venice Biennale and Gropius Bau), opera and theater direction, and gallery-based sculpture and video. This is her third solo exhibition with the gallery, following A Day in the Life of Bliss (2014) and Lovesong (2021), and arrives as part of Berlin Art Week's Gallery Night.

Given Tsang's history of working across disciplines — film, sculpture, live performance, and now this gallery presentation — expect a show that resists a single medium, using the idea of the metic as a lens on displacement, identity, and the porous line between insider and outsider.

shows.title: The Seed Is the Tree Is the House
shows.artist: Šejla Kamerić, Verena Melgarejo Weinandt, Grit Richter, Cielo Saucedo, Anna Steinert & Angelika J. Trojnarski
shows.description:
This group show brings together six artists whose work treats matter as process rather than fixed substance — a rebuttal, as the gallery frames it, to the old Western habit of carving the world into stable, measurable things. Šejla Kamerić's brass thorn-branch sculptures and body-based photographs sit alongside Verena Melgarejo Weinandt's textile installation built from entretela, the interlining fabric she uses as a metaphor for cultural in-betweenness. Grit Richter contributes her signature incandescent, grid-based oil paintings, hovering between the digital, the atomic and the cosmic.

Cielo Saucedo's 3D-printed self-portrait sculpture, cast in a hacked mixture of corn masa, clay and self-tanner, extends her ongoing research into NAFTA-era labor and border politics, while Anna Steinert shows paintings, masks and sculptural "creatures" that draw on feminist speculative fiction. Angelika J. Trojnarski rounds out the show with new paintings developed from her expeditions to glaciers and forests, where exposed, unpainted canvas becomes as important to the composition as the pigment itself.

Together the works propose ecology, cybernetics and non-Western cosmologies as better models for thinking about matter than the hard boundaries of classical science — treating trees, seeds, houses, bodies and borders as stages in the same continuous process rather than separate categories. The show opens during Berlin Art Week, with a performance by Anna Steinert and Sophie Labrey on the opening night.

shows.title: The New England Paintings
shows.description:
Timed to Berlin Art Week, this show gathers roughly a dozen small, plein-air paintings that the American painter Jim Butler has made over the past five years in his native northern New England. Butler paints directly from observation, and the pictures on view stay close to that scale of attention: rivers, trees, boats and shifting light rendered with an intimacy that owes as much to memory as to landscape painting tradition.

Butler, who trained at RISD and Indiana University and has shown steadily in New York and New England since the 1980s, works in a register that favors quiet accumulation over spectacle. The paintings' modest size asks for close looking, and their handling of atmosphere and color carries a stillness that feels deliberately at odds with the pace of an art-fair week. It's a small, unshowy show, but a good one for anyone wanting a breather from the bigger Gallery Weekend spectacles nearby.

shows.title: New Systems (For Relationships)
shows.description:
Lúcia Koch turns the gallery into a walk-through diagram of color and proximity for this Berlin Art Week opening. The Brazilian artist, long interested in architecture as a language rather than a container, presents mobile structures hung with dyed, translucent fabric filters — curved and straight rail-mounted modules that visitors move through, around and inside.

The work, part of an ongoing series Koch has developed since 2022, depends on the presence of the audience to complete it: every crossing of a fabric panel changes the color relationships in the room, so the piece behaves less like a fixed installation than an evolving field of encounters between bodies, light and translucent color. It follows earlier iterations of this curtain-filter strategy shown at Palais de Iéna in Paris and the Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah, and continues Koch's long-running interest in filtering perception of architectural space through color and transparency rather than solid form.

For anyone who has found Koch's photographic and sculptural interventions in previous shows cerebral to the point of coolness, this body of work is markedly more physical and social — an installation that only really exists once people start moving through it.

shows.title: Animal Mirror
shows.description:
A thirteen-artist group show built around the oldest, most contradictory relationship humans have with another species: the animal as companion and as commodity, as myth-carrier and as mirror for our own instincts. Rather than settling into single-issue advocacy, the exhibition lets very different practices talk past and around each other — Aki Inomata's work made in literal collaboration with living creatures sits alongside Lin May Saeed's sculptural meditations on animal liberation and Thomas Schütte and Asta Gröting's more visceral, grotesque takes on the body.

Painters Diego Delas, Paolo Salvador and Sequoia Scavullo contribute dreamlike scenes where human and animal figures blur into one another, while Paloma Varga Weisz and Julia Kowalska draw on older traditions of hybrid, fabled creatures. Ceramic, sculptural and sound-based work by Thibault Hiss, Jelena Bulajić and David Zink Yi rounds out the show with more material approaches to animal presence.

What holds the show together is a refusal of tidy moralizing — the artists here are more interested in the discomfort of the gaze we return to animals than in delivering a verdict on it. Opening for Berlin Art Week, it's a smart, wide-ranging group show that rewards slow looking across very different media.

shows.title: Lockruf der Sirenen. Visionen eines Seemanns
shows.description:
Valentina Murabito has spent over two decades pushing photography off the two-dimensional page, and this exhibition — its title translates loosely as "Siren Song: A Sailor's Visions" — gathers new work in which photographic images are fused onto unconventional supports and materials to become physical, almost sculptural objects. Analog color photographs printed onto watercolor paper, works that read as much as objects to be handled and lit from different angles as images to be looked at flatly, run through the show.

The maritime and mythological imagery in the titles — sirens, sea women, midnight flight — signals Murabito's long-running interest in transformation and liminal states, themes that recur through figures caught mid-metamorphosis, faces doubled or split, and bodies rendered ambiguous between human and mythic creature. Her choice of hand-applied, one-of-a-kind processes stands in deliberate opposition to the infinitely reproducible, weightless nature of digital photography — every print here is materially singular.

For a gallery whose program leans toward painting and object-based practice, this is a chance to see photography handled as a genuinely sculptural medium, where surface, texture and the physical presence of the print matter as much as the picture it carries.

shows.title: Strawalde. Parade
shows.description:
Strawalde is the painting alias of Jürgen Böttcher, a figure who lived two full careers in East German culture — as a filmmaker and documentarian under his given name, and as a painter under his pseudonym after the GDR's artists' union expelled him for "formalism." This Berlin Art Week solo show, timed to the artist's presence at the opening, gathers three decades of his thickly worked, gesturally built paintings, from a 1990 pair of large collage-and-oil canvases made in Paris to portraits and figure studies completed as recently as 2023 and 2024.

The paintings on view move between recognizable subjects — beach scenes, portraits, a self-described "Parade" of masked or costumed figures — and passages that dissolve into pure paint handling: fabric, buttons, Velcro, coins and other materials worked into the canvas alongside oil. Titles are mostly dated rather than named, a diaristic habit that underscores how much these pictures function as a working notebook spanning half a century, made largely outside the West German gallery system until reunification let Strawalde exhibit freely.

It's a rare chance to see a substantial survey of an artist more discussed than shown outside Germany, with a catalogue accompanying the exhibition.

shows.title: Containing the Container
shows.description:
Turin-born, New York-based Luisa Rabbia has spent three decades working across drawing, sculpture and painting to probe questions of intimacy, memory and the body, often building up her surfaces from obsessive fields of colored pencil, thread and paint that read almost like topographical maps of feeling. Containing the Container, timed to open during Berlin Art Week, is her first show with Tanya Leighton and gathers new paintings and sculptural work that push at the idea of the body — or any vessel — as something porous rather than sealed.

The title plays on a central tension in Rabbia's practice: the desire to hold and protect versus the impossibility of ever fully containing a life, a memory, or a relationship. Recent bodies of work by the artist have taken on titles like "Hidden Lives" and "Pieta," suggesting a continued interest in caretaking, loss and the maternal, themes that recur across the intimately worked surfaces on view here — some pieces read as quasi-figurative studies of embrace and enclosure, others as more abstract fields built from accumulated marks.

Rabbia has shown at institutions including the Lentos Kunstmuseum in Linz and Collezione Maramotti in Reggio Emilia, and her work rewards close, patient looking — the kind of attention that a small gallery show, rather than a museum survey, makes possible. This is a good opportunity to catch an under-the-radar figure just as she's getting wider attention in Europe.
