shows.title: From the Sleep Side
shows.description:
This Berlin Art Week show puts the American painter Aubrey Levinthal in direct dialogue with two artists she names as key influences: the Polish-American modernist Biala (Janice Biala, 1903-2000) and the Danish painter Tal R. It's a smart piece of curatorial matchmaking — Levinthal's tilted, cropped domestic interiors (a bathtub ledge, a mirror fogged with implication, a figure glimpsed through geraniums) share a vocabulary of skewed perspective and half-withheld intimacy with Biala's loosely structured still lifes and Tal R's folk-inflected, dreamlike scenes.

The show's title borrows from the poet Anne Carson's account of a dream in which a familiar room, entered "from the sleep side," becomes uncannily unfamiliar despite nothing being out of place. That sense of the ordinary tipping into the strange runs through all three artists' work here, whether in Biala's half-adrift still-life objects, Tal R's painted-over mirrors and curtained thresholds, or Levinthal's recurring motif of closed eyes and obscured reflections.

Notably, this marks only the second time Biala's work has been shown in Berlin — the first was in 1966 — making the show as much a rediscovery of an under-recognized modernist as a showcase for a rising contemporary painter and her sources.

shows.title: "Souvenirs de vacances" | Gallery Cabinet
shows.artist: Katherine Bradford, Daniel Hauptmann, Maximilian Kirmse, Heidrun Rathgeb
shows.description:
A small-format group presentation in the gallery's Cabinet space, timed to Berlin Art Week under a title that translates as "holiday souvenirs." Katherine Bradford contributes one of her signature pared-down, sun-bleached figure paintings — swimmers reduced to simple silhouettes against a pier — while Maximilian Kirmse shows a run of oil-crayon works on paper with the loose, quick touch of a sketchbook.

Heidrun Rathgeb's small egg-tempera panels bring a different register entirely: jewel-toned nocturnes with titles like "Norwegische Nacht" and "Abendstern" that read more as devotional objects than postcards, working in a slow, historically-rooted medium against the show's breezier vacation theme. Taken together the works trade on the gap between the souvenir as souvenir and the souvenir as a genuinely worked, considered object — appropriate for a cabinet show built for close, unhurried looking.

shows.title: Life–Death
shows.description:
At the center of this Berlin Art Week show is a 16mm film Katharina Sieverding made in 1969, shown at documenta 5 three years later — a work she made as a young student of Joseph Beuys in Düsseldorf, in the middle of the academy protests and nightlife scene that fed her early aesthetic. The film abandons narrative for a sequence of portraits and body studies in which Sieverding and collaborators appear in heavy makeup and androgynous costume, holding masculine and feminine, life and death, movement and stillness in unresolved tension — an early, prescient take on gender performance decades before the term existed.

The gallery pairs the dual-channel projection with large-format film stills and previously unpublished Polaroids, giving weight to the photographic residue of a work that was, in 1972, given a new soundtrack recorded in a single studio session by the not-yet-famous members of Kraftwerk — a detail that places the film at a genuine hinge point between rock, early electronic music and performance art.

Seen today, amid AI-generated imagery and algorithmic visibility, Sieverding's questions about how identity is constructed through images feel freshly relevant rather than merely historical, and this show is a rare chance to see a foundational work of her career in depth rather than as a single icon.

shows.title: Die Sein: Para Psychics Expanded (Excerpt)
shows.description:
Kerstin Brätsch's first solo show with the gallery turns the Corner Space and adjacent window into a single, mutating organism built from the vocabulary of her painting practice pushed into architecture. A patterned vinyl floor — derived from a stone-mosaic design that itself descends from her stucco marmo works and, before that, her oil paintings on Mylar — acts as a connective surface running between the gallery's two window spaces, catching and transforming light as it shifts through the day.

Large cardboard panels enlarge motifs from Brätsch's stucco marmo pieces (a centuries-old technique for imitating marble in plaster, pigment and glue), their organic forms drifting between geode-like patterning and half-glimpsed faces. Hung against this backdrop is a small selection from her ongoing "Para Psychics" series — an eventual body of one hundred colored-pencil drawings whose mandala-like, asymmetrical patterns loosely reference tarot and other systems of divination, built up through layering and erasure.

Brätsch has long treated painting as raw material to be broken down and reassembled across media rather than a fixed endpoint, and this show is a compact but ambitious demonstration of that logic — less an exhibition of finished paintings than an immersive diagram of how one image keeps becoming another.

shows.title: Nachtruhe
shows.description:
David L. Johnson builds this show around the quiet infrastructure that governs who gets to occupy public space after dark — sound works, subtractive sculpture, printed matter and photography made in and around parks in Philadelphia, New York and Berlin. The starting points are specific and bureaucratic: Philadelphia's minors' curfew code and the "Mosquito" high-frequency sound deterrents installed in over thirty of its parks since 2014; the 1988 Tompkins Square Park curfew riots and the privately policed "POPS" spaces that followed in New York; and, closer to home, Görlitzer Park's contested status as one of Berlin's designated kriminalitätsbelasteter Orte, where police can search without individual suspicion.

Johnson treats these overlapping histories of curfews, sonic deterrents and surveilled green space as material rather than illustration — the show's title, German for "night's rest" or officially mandated quiet hours, sits ironically atop a body of work about who is denied rest, and where. The Görlitzer Park material is especially timely: a nighttime closure imposed by Berlin's Senate in March 2026 was suspended by the Administrative Court in June, though the physical gates remain installed while the case continues.

It's a research-dense show, but one that stays grounded in Johnson's sculptural and photographic eye for the specific hardware — gates, floodlights, sensors — that quietly reshapes who can be in public after dark.

shows.title: Sugarshack
shows.description:
Salim Green's first European solo show takes its title from a term his father used for abandoned or run-down buildings in Waterloo, Iowa, a Midwestern industrial town that drew Black families north during the Great Migration, many recruited to work the railroads, and housed them first in boxcars and then in segregated neighborhoods now dotted with vacant lots. Green treats the term less as nostalgia than as a way of measuring a community's vitality through its built environment.

The installation centers on the fellowship hall of Payne Memorial AME, a historically Black church on Waterloo's east side, a secondary space that absorbs and holds the residue of community gatherings when they're not in session. Green translates that space into a new body of drawings, sculptures and video, including a piece featuring his recurring CGI avatar Shifty, here recast as a race-shifting Iowa farmer who narrates the railroad's history with the town and drifts through the installation as a kind of haunting presence.

Green works from speculative frameworks like Dark Forest Theory, using concealment and illegibility as deliberate strategies rather than obstacles, an approach that runs through his small-scale abstractions as much as through this more narrative, site-specific installation. The show also marks the start of a residency at Callie's, Berlin, later this fall.

shows.title: Park by POCO
shows.description:
Gregor Hildebrandt returns to Wentrup with a new body of work that takes the garden as its organizing metaphor — not a literal plot of earth but what he calls the gardens of the soul, the private plantings of memory built from music, film, and literature. Hildebrandt has spent two decades working with the detritus of analog media: cassette tape, vinyl records, and VHS stock peeled apart and pressed into monochrome surfaces so that a beloved album or film becomes, quite literally, the pigment of a painting. That process — excavation and transformation of obsolete recording formats into abstract fields — remains his signature move, and it is easy to see why: the tape's sheen and the ghost of its former sound give the work a melancholic, nostalgic charge that pure abstraction can't match.

The garden framework lets Hildebrandt widen his usual references (Nick Cave collaborator Blixa Bargeld gets a nod alongside Voltaire's Candide and the biblical Eden) into ideas of growth, accumulation and renewal, suggesting a show more expansive and additive than his tighter, more elegiac past bodies of work. Expect large-format tape paintings alongside sculptural or object-based pieces that continue his interest in the material residue of listening and watching.

For longtime followers of Hildebrandt this is a chance to see how a well-worn conceptual engine — pop culture as raw material — gets pointed toward something more pastoral and cyclical. For newcomers it's a good entry point into one of Berlin's most consistently poetic image-makers, whose work rewards close, patient looking at surfaces that reveal themselves to be built from a thousand small cuts of magnetic tape.

shows.title: Return to Content a/b
shows.description:
Julia Wachtel has spent four decades mining the visual detritus of mass media — tabloid photography, cartoon characters, advertising, celebrity portraiture — and pairing it against itself in jarring, silkscreen-inflected paintings. This show, her first comprehensive solo presentation in Germany, gathers new oil, acrylic and silkscreen canvases that continue that project: images torn from an image-saturated world and recombined so their original meanings curdle into something stranger.

Wachtel emerged in early-1980s New York alongside the Pictures Generation, artists preoccupied with how mass media manufactures and recycles imagery, and her work has always operated by collision — a cartoon figure set against a documentary photograph, high finish against flat commercial gloss. Seeing the paintings in person makes clear how physical that collision is: passages of loose, almost gestural paint sit right up against hard-edged printed color, so the canvas itself seems to argue with its own sources.

The exhibition runs concurrently with a companion presentation at Jahn und Jahn in Munich, both accompanied by a text from critic Jens Asthoff, underscoring how Wachtel's pictures function serially — as an ongoing index of the culture's visual noise rather than a single fixed statement. It's a rare chance to see a foundational Pictures Generation artist's work at scale in Berlin.
shows.reception: Berlin Art Week opening; artist talk with Julia Wachtel and Philipp Hindahl on September 12 at 4pm

shows.title: tracks, taps
shows.description:
Downstairs at Klemm's, this two-person show pairs Mia Gap and Freja Sofie Kirk around a shared question: what happens to desire once it's been thoroughly mediated by screens? Gap works by pushing digitally conceived imagery back into physical form — panels that read like renderings but insist on their own material presence. Kirk works the opposite direction, using cinematic and sensorial strategies to pry images loose from the flat rectangle of the frame, twisting perception until the two-dimensional picture plane starts to feel unstable.

Curated by the gallery's own Guilherme Vilhena Martins, the exhibition sits deliberately between Gap's object-making and Kirk's more atmospheric, moving-image sensibility, letting exhaustion and seduction trade places throughout the space. It's a compact, sharply pitched show about what's left of the image once materiality, simulation and fatigue have all had their say — a fitting companion to the Julia Wachtel survey upstairs, which is interested in adjacent territory from an earlier media moment.

Opening during Berlin Art Week, tracks, taps is a good entry point into two younger practices worth tracking as the gallery's downstairs program continues to platform emerging positions alongside its established roster.

shows.title: Stolon
shows.description:
Azade Köker takes her title from botany: a stolon is a runner that a plant sends out along the ground rather than down into the earth, rooting new growth at its nodes before dying back. It's an apt image for a show built almost entirely from paper, wire and thread — materials that are provisional, light, and endlessly extendable. At the center of the exhibition is a forest of thirteen tall paper columns wound like bark and hung from the ceiling on near-invisible threads, so that they sway with the room's air currents; from the top of each, a twisted paper strand descends to tangle with its neighbors on the floor, turning a classical architectural motif — the column, the caryatid — into something more like a nervous system.

Köker has spent five decades moving between hard and soft registers: from early terracotta figures addressing women's labor (a piece dealing with Turkish "guest workers" recruited to West Berlin factories is a career touchstone, later recast in bronze for a Gropius Bau show) to the paper and wire she has favored since the 1990s, which she treats as a kind of skin — permeable, foldable, holding the memory of every crease. Stolon extends that material logic into new sculptural works using garden and fencing wire bent into synapse-like branching structures, illuminated strips of light standing in for the electrical charge of a nervous system, plus a large paper sphere caught in a net inscribed with the word "ICH" (self), and a series of small collaged figures that blur human, animal and plant forms.

Thematically the show sits at the intersection of care and constraint — the double meaning of "holding," a net that can rescue or trap — and it's a good showcase of how a long, quietly influential career keeps finding new material metaphors for old questions about the body, gender, and social bonds. A catalogue with essays by Simon O'Sullivan and Lotte Laub accompanies the show.

shows.title: Echotropia
shows.description:
Christian Achenbach's third show with König is built around a single monumental canvas, Genesis, made specifically for the soaring Nave of St. Agnes — the kind of scale that only a former church can accommodate. Achenbach paints in a deliberately unnatural palette of burning reds, saturated oranges, deep blues and acid greens, laying wavy, rhythmic bands of color across the surface until landscape dissolves into something closer to a musical score, light and shape reverberating rather than sitting still.

Trained in Berlin under Daniel Richter and Anselm Reyle, Achenbach works squarely in the tradition of landscape painting while refusing its usual calm — his color is structural rather than descriptive, organizing the composition almost the way a beat organizes a piece of music. In Genesis, an abstract grid pattern in the foreground nods to the enlargement grids Renaissance painters used to scale up sketches, a small technical joke about how his own oversized gesture gets built.

The result is a show about echo and territory without a map — Achenbach placing himself, half-seriously, within a lineage of landscape and color-field painting he's simultaneously extending and unsettling.

shows.title: The Archaeology of Beasts
shows.description:
Monira Al Qadiri's practice has long circled the "petro-culture" of the Gulf, using speculative sci-fi imagery to pick apart statecraft, gender and modernization. For this show — her third with König, staged in the Chapel of St. Agnes — she turns further back in time, to ancient Egypt, tracing the same questions about power, hierarchy and the boundary between human, animal and divine through a much older civilization's own image system.

The exhibition, first shown at Bozar in Brussels in 2024, brings together glossy black sculptures, video and a virtual-reality piece. At the entrance, two ready-made figures — Automaton — represent Khnum and Anubis, gods of creation and mummification, silently rotating in a kind of mechanical dialogue. A video work, Book of the Dead, animates 3D scans of Luxor statues reciting funerary spells, while the VR piece Aaru: After Lament drops viewers into a golden wheat field modeled on the ancient Egyptian idea of paradise — an infinite, harmonious Nile Delta whose eventual flooding reads easily as a climate-crisis metaphor.

It's a show about how deeply the ancient Egyptians entangled nature, animals, cultivated land and human labor — and an argument, via Al Qadiri's characteristically sleek, faintly uncanny sculptural language, that those entanglements never really went away.

shows.title: The Last Ones Awake
shows.description:
Rebecca Brodskis paints the people who became her family in Berlin. Installed in the Vault of St. Agnes, this solo show gathers oil-on-linen portraits of the friends she made during the years she lived in the city in the mid-2000s, when cheap apartments and coal-heated flats still made room for a close, improvised community of young artists far from home.

Rather than documenting a scene, Brodskis paints the quiet, suspended interiority of individual relationships — figures caught mid-thought, their expressions resisting any clear narrative but carrying the weight of years of shared history. Works like Pass This On and The Last Ones Awake read less as portraits of specific people than as fragments of a collective memory, the residue of friendships that had to bear the weight of kinship because actual family was elsewhere.

Brodskis, who first encountered Berlin through Annemarie Schwarzenbach's writing as a teenager in France, is explicit that the show mourns a version of the city that no longer exists — not through nostalgia, but as a clear-eyed record of what it took, and what it gave, to build an artistic life on very little. A performance by the Greek dancer Aurora accompanies the opening.
shows.reception: Berlin Art Week opening, September 8, 2026, 6-9pm, with a performance by Aurora at 7pm

shows.title: Circle Paintings
shows.description:
Alan Charlton has painted almost nothing but grey monochrome canvases since the early 1970s, treating the color as a way to strip painting down to its bare structural facts — support, surface, edge, shadow. This show, staged for Berlin Art Week's Gallery Night, shifts his usual rectangular format into the circle, a shape that changes how the paintings sit against the wall and against each other, replacing the grid-like logic of his rectangular works with something more like a constellation.

Charlton emerged in London in the 1970s in the wake of minimalism, but his gray is not really about absence — it's a deliberately narrow field within which every variable that remains (scale, thickness, the gap between two canvases, the way light catches a rounded edge differently than a straight one) becomes newly legible. Seeing his circular works alongside Martin Margiela's concurrent show in the same gallery makes for a suggestive pairing: two artists who have each built entire practices out of extreme reduction and repetition, one in painting and one in fashion-turned-fine-art.

It's a rare chance to see a substantial body of new work from an artist whose career has been defined by patient, incremental variation on a single idea.

shows.title: Martin Margiela in Berlin
shows.description:
Martin Margiela's second career, as a fine artist following his years as the anonymity-obsessed force behind Maison Margiela, has centered on sculpture and installation that treats the body, textiles and domestic objects with the same forensic, slightly uncanny attention he once brought to garment construction. This exhibition, opening alongside Alan Charlton's Circle Paintings for Berlin Art Week's Gallery Night, marks Margiela's continuing relationship with Konrad Fischer Galerie and gives Berlin a substantial look at where that second practice has landed.

Margiela's transition from fashion to art was never simply a change of medium — his fashion work was already conceptual, built on deconstruction, erasure and the refusal of authorial branding, so his gallery work reads as a continuation of the same questions by other means: what a body is, what wear and repair look like, how an object accrues or loses meaning through display. Expect the same rigor and dry humor that made his fashion house legendary, now applied to sculpture and objects rather than clothing.

Paired with Charlton's monochrome circles in the gallery's raw, historically protected former electrical substation, the two shows share a formal austerity even as they come from entirely different disciplines — a smart piece of programming for Gallery Night.

shows.title: Rhizome
shows.description:
Paweł Książek works across two registers that don't usually sit in the same room: precise black-and-white drawing and full-color painting. This show, opening during Berlin Art Week, brings both together — the artist's ongoing Narrations series of drawings alongside a new group of paintings — and lets them talk to each other rather than presenting a single tidy argument.

The title is apt. Rather than building toward one linear narrative, the exhibition unfolds more like a network of associations, where recurring motifs resurface across mediums and gain new inflections each time. Książek's control of line, tone and light gives even his most fragmentary images real weight, and the dialogue between text and image that runs through his drawings extends into the paintings as a kind of visual grammar rather than illustration.

For a gallery long associated with the Helsinki School's photography-based program, a show built around drawing and painting is a notable departure — worth seeing both for Książek's technical command and for what it signals about where Persons Projects is taking its exhibition program.
shows.reception: Thursday, September 10, 2026, 6-10pm, as part of Berlin Art Week 2026

shows.title: Hollywood Forever
shows.description:
Kate Mosher Hall paints in acrylic and flashe with a flattened, screen-printed quality that makes her canvases read like stills pulled from an unplaceable broadcast — faces and figures rendered in high-contrast tonal blocks that recall halftone printing and analog television static as much as they do painting. Hollywood Forever, her show at Trautwein Herleth, brings together new large-scale canvases that continue this interrogation of mediated imagery and Americana.

The title nods to the Los Angeles cemetery of the same name, a place where celebrity, mortality and myth-making sit side by side, and that tension runs through the work: images that feel iconic and half-erased at once, as if memory and mass media were compressing a figure down to its most legible silhouette. Mosher Hall's palette — often reduced to a few sharp tones — heightens the sense that these are images already once removed, processed through a lens of reproduction before they ever reached canvas.

Los Angeles–based Mosher Hall has been gaining steady attention for a painting practice that treats commercial image-making as raw material rather than target, and this Berlin outing gives a European audience a substantial look at where that project stands.

shows.title: Modul im Modell
shows.description:
Sinta Werner builds her sculptures and photographic works out of the vocabulary of modernist architecture — grids, glass panes, scaffolding, and the kind of orderly geometry that once promised rational, stable space. In this show she takes that vocabulary apart. Glass recurs throughout as a literal and conceptual device: it reflects, refracts and layers, so that a wall or a floor plan never quite resolves into a single legible image.

What's distinctive about Werner's approach is that the destabilization is bodily rather than purely optical. The works are built to be walked around — a shift in eye level or a step to the side changes what a structure appears to be, turning the gallery visit itself into the subject of the piece. It's an approach she has developed over shows at institutions like the Bauhaus-Archiv and Schloss Biesdorf, and this exhibition (titled, roughly, "Module in the Model") reads as a concentrated study of architectural models made unstable.

For anyone interested in the overlap between sculpture, photography and architecture, this is a tightly focused, single-artist show rather than a survey — a good entry point into how Werner thinks through space using very simple materials.

shows.title: The lie, the larp and the lusophile
shows.description:
Austin Martin White's second solo show with the gallery spans its entire exhibition space and centers on the Brazilian Baroque sculptor Antônio Francisco Lisboa — known as Aleijadinho — whose life has always sat somewhere between documented fact and legend. White paints portraits of the artist and his famous prophet sculptures at the Sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Matosinhos, alongside works that borrow the graphic language of literatura de cordel, the cheap illustrated pamphlets that have carried folklore, religion and politics through Northeastern Brazil for generations.

The paintings themselves are built from unglamorous, semi-industrial materials — polyethylene film, screen mesh, rubber, vinyl, spray paint — layered in a way that mimics how historical images actually reach us: filtered, reprinted, degraded, retouched. That's the real subject here: not Aleijadinho's biography so much as the mechanics by which a national myth gets manufactured and passed down, and what happens to a colonial history once it's been run through the mediating screens of print and folklore.

White, a Detroit-born, Philadelphia-based painter, has shown at Capitain Petzel before and has had solo outings at Petzel's New York space; his work sits in the Hessel Museum's permanent collection and has drawn attention in Artforum, Texte zur Kunst and elsewhere. This show is a good chance to see how an American painter works through Latin American postcolonial material without simply illustrating it — the layered, semi-industrial surfaces do a lot of the argument's heavy lifting.

shows.title: Pleiades
shows.description:
Achraf Touloub returns to Plan B's Berlin space with a new body of oil paintings named for the Pleiades star cluster, a fitting title for an artist whose work has long moved between the intimate and the cosmic. Touloub, who has shown with the gallery since 2014 with exhibitions like "European Night" and "Latent," works in a spare, atmospheric register — figures and landscapes rendered with a kind of nocturnal clarity, as if lit by starlight rather than sun.

One anchor work, "La source (Aïn Diab)," points to the Moroccan coast — Aïn Diab is a beach district of Casablanca — suggesting the show continues Touloub's interest in North African light and memory filtered through a muted, painterly palette. Expect a tight body of canvases rather than a sprawling installation: this is a gallery known for a slow, considered relationship with a small roster of painters, and Touloub's shows here have always rewarded close, quiet looking over spectacle.

shows.title: Exuvie
shows.description:
Marie Schubert's first show at the gallery, opening during Berlin Art Week, takes its title from "exuvia" — the shed husks insects leave behind, still bearing the shape of a creature that's long gone. Schubert applies that idea to objects loaded with status and vanity: a hollowed-out Lotus Elan +2 sports car, sandblasted until it's translucent and stripped of its engine and seats, stands as an emptied-out trophy of masculinity and luxury. Nearby, bronze-cast wigs — modeled on everything from Louis XIV's allongé style to Marie Antoinette's towering coiffure — turn a Baroque symbol of vanity and power into inert, gleaming relics.

Elsewhere the show works in a quieter register: sequins from a suit of armor, a cut-open bag, drawings in which dollar signs float free and frogs sun themselves next to blister packs of headache pills. Across all of it, Schubert is interested in what remains once an object's function and context are stripped away — the husk that keeps a "lingering sense of vitality" even after everything essential is gone.

Schubert, born in Düsseldorf in 1995, graduated this year from the Düsseldorf Art Academy under Alexandra Bircken, whose interest in the body and materiality is a clear touchstone here. This is a promising, formally sharp debut for a young sculptor working the line between craft object, cultural artifact and elegy.

shows.title: Handmade by—Part II
shows.artist: Georg Haberler, Seet van Hout, Bouthayna Al Muftah, Sergio Roger, Magda Sayeg, Yukiko Terada, Joana Vasconcelos, Gerhard Kehl, Patricia Waller
shows.description:
Nine years after its first "Handmade by" show, Galerie Deschler returns to the relationship between art and textile technique with a second, more international edition curated by the gallery's own crochet artist, Patricia Waller. The thread — literally and as metaphor — ties together wildly different practices: Sergio Roger's antique-linen-wrapped classical columns and busts, Joana Vasconcelos's crocheted-lace-trimmed Portuguese faience objects, Yukiko Terada's sashiko-stitched embroidery hoops, Magda Sayeg's yarn-bombed "Machine Gun," and Bouthayna Al Muftah's ink-and-thread works from her series on Qatari women's hair rituals.

Threaded through the textile pieces are carved wooden sculptures by Gerhard Kehl, who died last year — his lacquered animal and opera-inspired figures giving the show a craft counterpoint that isn't textile at all, but shares its handmade, patient physicality. The result is less a survey of "textile art" as a genre than an argument for craft itself as a way of thinking: repetition and patience set against improvisation and chance, with each artist finding a different way to make meaning out of accumulated, repeated gesture.

It's a warm, tactile show, heavier on pattern and color than the gallery's sometimes darker programming, and a good one for visitors curious about where fiber art currently sits between craft, sculpture and painting.

shows.title: hook, line and sinker
shows.description:
Stef Heidhues starts from objects so familiar they barely register — safety goggles, a saddle, styrofoam packing forms, advertising signs — and puts each through a strange process of transformation: she scans an object to capture its exact form and surface, then rebuilds it by hand in a new material, so that the original's traces survive inside something that no longer functions as the thing it was. Cast bronze safety goggles become a swarm of insect-like twin forms; a polymer-gypsum saddle reads equally as a bird spreading its wings; aluminum casts of foam packing material, once anonymous protective padding, become frames in their own right.

The show's title piece, a vastly scaled-up fishing hook complete with line and sinker, gives a name to the exhibition's real subject: the moment of falling for what a form promises, of being pulled along by an object's seductive surface even after you know it's hollow. Running alongside the sculptural works is "No Sign," an ongoing series of wall signs bearing paired words or phrases — commands, non-sequiturs, fragments of overheard language — that refuse to give the clarity a sign is supposed to provide.

Heidhues's work sits at the intersection of readymade and craft: nothing here is simply found, but nothing is invented from scratch either. It's a quietly cerebral show about presence and absence, well suited to slow looking — the kind of exhibition where knowing what an object used to be changes how you see what it's become. It opens during Berlin Art Week.

shows.title: The Image Is a Public Menace
shows.description:
Abdulnasser Gharem, a former lieutenant colonel in the Saudi Arabian army turned one of the Gulf's most prominent contemporary artists, presents three new projects built around a single, loaded anecdote: in 2015 he smuggled a female mannequin into Riyadh — where such figures were considered inappropriate — by having it cut into pieces in Dubai and reassembled once inside the country. He then staged a re-enactment of Martin Ferdinand Quadal's 1787 painting "The Nude Drawing Room of the Vienna Academy" with fellow artists, restaging a European academic history-painting scene around a contraband object.

For this exhibition Gharem pushes the story another step: he commissioned a Vienna-trained copyist to repaint his 2015 photograph in Quadal's own 18th-century technique, documenting the whole process on video, and produced a second large-format painting depicting the moment his collaborators assembled the mannequin. The result — titled "Aniconism," after the historic practice of avoiding figurative religious imagery — collapses history painting, performance documentation and contemporary political smuggling into a single, layered object, asking pointed questions about who gets to control an image as it moves between cultures.

Heimo Zobernig, who exhibited alongside Gharem at the Sharjah Art Museum in 2018, designed the installation using his signature green-screen "Trevira" curtains — a nod to obsolete film technology in an exhibition otherwise concerned with how images travel and mutate. It's a dense, research-driven show from an artist whose stamped, bureaucratic aesthetic has long taken on Gulf politics obliquely; this one is more directly about the mechanics of image-making itself.

shows.title: Half-Life of Grace
shows.description:
Jeremy Shaw's work has circled the same territory for two decades: altered states, belief systems, and the technologies — scientific, religious, chemical, cinematic — that people use to try to get outside of ordinary consciousness. The Vancouver-born, Berlin-based artist typically works through faux-documentary video, manipulated found footage and sculptural installation, staging his subjects (ravers, cultists, meditators) with the visual grammar of ethnographic or scientific record, then destabilizing that grammar until the footage itself starts to glitch, blur or hallucinate.

"Half-Life of Grace" — the title alone suggests something measurable decaying, an ecstatic state with a measurable decay rate — continues that inquiry. Shaw has had institutional solo shows at the Centre Pompidou, Schinkel Pavillon and MoMA PS1, and represented strong company at the 57th Venice Biennale and Manifesta 11; this Berlin gallery show is a chance to see a tighter, more concentrated body of new work outside the museum context.

Given Shaw's history of pairing scientific-looking apparatus with genuinely uncanny visual effects, expect the show to blend video, photography and sculptural elements rather than sit as a single medium — and expect it to reward the kind of slow, repeat viewing his looping video works are built for.

shows.title: Shimmer
shows.artist: Noémi Barbaglia, Noi Fuhrer, Rosa Lüders
shows.description:
Shimmer brings together three artists whose work circles around the instability of images — how pictures are built, what they leave out, and how they slip between record and invention. The premise is broad enough to hold quite different practices: Rosa Lüders' small, glossy paint-on-aluminium panels (one included here, Sizzling Hot (burning plums), turns a mundane still-life motif into something closer to a glitch or afterimage), alongside Noi Fuhrer's large charcoal drawings, which the gallery has previously described as having a sculptural, almost phantasmagoric presence, and Noémi Barbaglia's contribution to the group.

Rather than a single argument, the show reads as a set of related questions — about perception, memory and dream-logic, and about what agency an image has once it starts to shape how we see rather than simply reflecting what's there. It's a compact, three-way conversation rather than a survey, typical of the modest, tightly-curated group shows this Mulackstraße gallery has built its reputation on.

Noi Fuhrer, born in Tel Aviv in 1987 and based in Berlin, studied at Goldsmiths in London and the Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg; her charcoal-on-paper works have become a recognizable part of the gallery's programme since she joined a few years ago. Barbaglia and Lüders round out the show as guest contributors, giving Shimmer the feel of a dialogue between an established gallery artist and two outside voices.

shows.title: Take Five
shows.description:
Michael Laube works in a lineage of hard-edged, geometric abstraction, building compositions out of taut, angular color fields whose diagonals and interlocking shapes keep the eye moving across the surface. His recent paintings — built from crisp, confidently cut planes of saturated color — sit in a tradition that runs from Constructivism through post-war concrete art, but Laube's own touch is drier and more graphic, closer to hard-edge design than to gestural painting.

Take Five is Laube's latest show with Kuckei + Kuckei, a gallery that has represented him for years alongside artists like Fiene Scharp and Gerhard Winkler working in related geometric and reductive idioms. Based on the works illustrated for the show, expect large-scale canvases in bold, contrasting palettes — reds, blacks, ochres and blues locked into sharp-angled, almost architectural arrangements.

Without extensive statement text from the gallery on this particular body of work, the strongest evidence for what's on view is the paintings themselves: rigorous, controlled abstractions that reward a slow look at how each color plane pushes against its neighbor.

shows.title: DIFFERENTLEVELSOFBEING
shows.description:
Markus Linnenbrink returns to Taubert Contemporary, the gallery that has shown his work since the early 2000s, with a new body of paintings and sculptural objects built from his signature material: pigmented epoxy resin poured, layered and worked over wood panels. The Dortmund-born, Brooklyn-based artist has spent three decades pushing that material past painting's usual limits, letting gravity and repeated pours generate dense vertical striations of color that he then cuts into, drills through or lets pool into low reliefs.

The title, run together in his usual all-caps shorthand, points to the show's premise of shifting registers — between flat surface and built-up sculptural mass, between the orderly stripe and the accidental drip. A newly surfacing work, HUMANSAREWEREADY?, gives a sense of the palette on view: hot, saturated color bands interrupted by passages where the resin has been ground back to expose earlier layers underneath, turning each panel into a kind of core sample of its own making.

Linnenbrink's lineage runs through American color-field abstraction — Morris Louis and Gene Davis are frequent reference points — filtered through a European, material-first sensibility indebted to artists like Jean Fautrier. What keeps his work interesting after so many exhibitions is the way process stays visible: every panel carries the evidence of pouring, waiting and cutting, so the finished surface reads less like an image than like a record of labor and time.

This is Linnenbrink's latest solo outing with the gallery and opens as part of Berlin Art Week, with extended hours during the fair days. It's a good entry point for anyone curious how far a single material — resin plus pigment — can be pushed across paintings, wall-based reliefs and freestanding pieces.

shows.title: Embodying Space
shows.dates_note: Gallery page lists 11 September – 16 October 2026, but the press text also names the opening reception 10 September 2026, 19:00, with special Berlin Art Week hours 10–14 September.
shows.description:
Two sculptors of hard materials share the gallery for this pairing of French object-maker Quentin Lefranc and Berlin-based painter-turned-sculptor Rainer Splitt. Both have spent decades working the seam between concrete art and minimalism, and the show reads as a study in how far reduction can go before it becomes something else entirely — Lefranc's cast and crushed forms (paper, cement, wood, steel) sit as isolated "monoliths" or theatrical props, while Splitt's floor and wall pieces work through pours and stacked planes that keep threatening to become paintings again.

Lefranc treats the gallery itself as raw material: his sculptures function like open brackets that test a room's permeability and its history rather than simply occupying it. Splitt, a Meisterschüler under Christiane Möbus with a museum exhibition history stretching from Schwerin to the Sprengel Museum Hanover, brings a quieter, more painterly discipline — pouring and layering rather than modeling — that plays off Lefranc's more sculptural, architectural gestures.

It's a smart two-hander for anyone interested in how concrete/minimal traditions have mutated in different hands: one artist pushing toward built environment and object, the other holding onto surface and color while still working in three dimensions.

venue.name: Galerie Gilla Lörcher
hours: During Berlin Art Week (10-14 Sep): Thu 6-10pm, Fri 12-8pm, Sat-Sun 12-6pm

shows.title: SEWING
shows.description:
Hannah Hallermann's solo show turns a piece of archery equipment into a sewing implement, using that transformation as the hinge for an installation that mixes archery gear, sculpture and textile work. The piece reads as a meditation on repair — taking an object built for aimed, single-directional force and repurposing it as a tool that joins things together instead of separating them.

The exhibition treats mending less as a fix than as a discipline: a way of paying close, sustained attention to tension and difference rather than resolving them. It's a tightly conceptual show built around one central gesture, which makes it a good fit for the collection's intimate exhibition space, and it opens right as Berlin Art Week brings extended hours and an artist talk to the space.

shows.title: Kritik und Selbstkritik in der freien Zeit | Criticism and Self-Criticism in Free Time
shows.description:
Leon Kahane's new body of work takes its title from the Marxist-Leninist concept of "criticism and self-criticism," pairing it with a deliberately double-edged idea of "free time" — as both a description of leisure and a loaded historical category shaped by competing political systems. The show spans photography, film and installation, and uses that tension to ask what remains of shifting political and institutional conditions in the images and memories artists leave behind.

Its anchor is Sport, Biology and Leisure, a 1970 public mural by Doris Kahane — the artist's mother — in Berlin-Johannisthal. Returning to that mural today, Kahane examines the position of the artist caught between political zeitgeist, state commission and personal conviction. He extends the inquiry outward to his own archive, bringing in photographs he took twenty years ago as a photojournalist in the West Bank, and an oral history interview with his grandfather recalling a childhood in the Scheunenviertel — the same historic quarter where the Kunstverein itself now sits, collapsing the distance between family history, East German cultural politics and the neighborhood outside the window.

Kahane, born in Berlin in 1985, trained in photography at the Ostkreuzschule and fine art at the UdK Berlin; his work has been shown at Kunsthalle Wien, the Jewish Museum Berlin, Belvedere 21 in Vienna and the Deichtorhallen Hamburg, and often returns to questions of European border politics and East German and Eastern European history filtered through his own biography. Alongside this solo show he is co-curating Projektionen auf den Osten with Fabian Bechtle at Schinkel Pavillon and n.b.k., making this a particularly active season for an artist whose work keeps circling back to how personal and political histories get inherited, revised and restaged.

shows.title: Projektionen auf den Osten (Projections onto the East)
shows.description:
Curators Fabian Bechtle and Leon Kahane split this group exhibition across two Mitte institutions — the Schinkel Pavillon and the Neuer Berliner Kunstverein a few streets away — to interrogate how "the East" gets imagined, flattened and mythologized as a foil to a hegemonic "West." The premise is pointed: rather than another retrospective survey of GDR nostalgia, the show treats "East" and "West" as ideological projection screens, tracing lines from Cold War-era image politics through post-socialist transformation to present-day geopolitical fault lines.

The artist list mixes historical and contemporary positions in a way that keeps the argument from settling into easy binaries. Helmar Lerski's interwar photographic studies of hands sit alongside Hito Steyerl's early video work and new pieces by Maya Schweizer, Maksym Khodak and Andrzej Steinbach, along with KwieKulik, Gabriele Stötzer, Mikhail Tolmachev, Jasmin Werner and others working across photography, 16mm and 4K film, and archival material.

Because it unfolds simultaneously at the Schinkel Pavillon and n.b.k., the show is conceived as much as a discursive project as an exhibition — accompanied by a publication, a project website and an extensive talks program addressing themes from antisemitism to postsocialist memory politics. The Schinkel Pavillon's octagonal, glass-walled hall — itself a piece of 1969 East German architecture — becomes an active participant in the argument rather than a neutral backdrop.

shows.title: Void is Seductive
shows.description:
Salomé Chatriot's second solo show at Office Impart centers on "First Month of Anger," a five-channel video installation following a transparent, headless CGI figure that exists purely as image — no interior, no exterior, just surface folded back on itself through inverted geometry and reflective render tricks. It's a body built to be looked at that can never quite be located.

Around the video, Chatriot extends the same logic into physical objects: new enamel paintings continue her glossy, hard-edged approach to figures rendered as if lit from inside a screen, and a leather sculpture titled "Void is Seductive 2" translates the video protagonist into something you could theoretically touch, collapsing the distance between avatar and object. The enamel-on-aluminum surface she's used in past works (all hard sheen, no brushwork) suits this concern with bodies as manufactured, mediated things.

Chatriot's work sits comfortably alongside a gallery program built around digital and post-internet image-making, and this show pushes that further into questions of visibility and desire under constant observation — a figure whose only mode of being is being seen, and who resents it.
